blocks.x: Let's see, this is an interview, a recording of music. We're making it today up at 1323 South Rampart Street. What's today's date? May the 12th. May the 12th, 1960. And my name is Dick Allen. What's yours name? Frank Murray. Frank Murray. M-U-R-R-A-Y. Murray, or Murray sometimes. Murray, yeah. And your name? Paul Crawford. Okay. You want to give us a little sample of the blues or something?

Well, a very old popular jazz song is Who's Sorry Now? Who's sorry now? Who's sorry now? Whose heart is breaking for a break in each bar? Who's sad and blue? Who's car in two? Just as I cried over you. Right from the start Just like a friend I tried to warn you somehow You had your way Now you must pray I'm glad that you'm sorry now Who's sorry now? Who's sorry now? Who's sorry now? Who's heart is crying? Just like I cried over you. Who's sad and blue? Who's crying too? Just like I cried over you. Who's dear to dear
You can turn back around to your same position where you were facing it.

Yeah, yeah. Missy Wood. How about that? C.C. Ryder. That's fine. C.C. Ryder, see what you done, done. Lord, Lord, you made me love you. Now your man done come. You made me love you. Now your man done come. Going away, baby. Won't be back to fall. Lord, Lord, I'm going away, baby. Won't be back to fall. If I find a good gal, won't be back at all. C.C. Ryder, see what you done, done. Lord, Lord, you made me love you. Now your man done come. You made me love you. Now your man done come. Cherokee Church by Cherokee Church I had a little bit of it.
Yeah, well that's good, no?
Yeah.
Okay. I'm tearing it up. Okay, let's go.

We play the game, Bob stay away. But it costs more than I can pay. Without you I can make my way. I surrender, dear. Living, amazing, gay. Not supposed to do that way. Cut deep down in my heart and say. I surrender, dear. Little mean things we were doing. That have been part of the game. Let them aspire to the moon. Don't care who to blame. When stars appear and shadows fall. To hear my poor boy call. To you my love, my life, my own. I surrender, dear. I surrender, dear. I surrender.
I surrender. I surrender. I surrender. I surrender. I surrender. Okay, we got your name. Yeah. And now come the personal questions. When were you born?

I was born in 1896. Exact birthday? What month? 1896, October the night. 1325 South, no, 12-0. I'm going to get my house ready. You know how it is in conversation. I'm on 1225 Eucousine Street. Where is that? That's where the IC railroad track goes out. See, that's all been demolished now. Howard Avenue was on the uptown side of the new basin and the old basin. On the downtown side of the new basin was Julia Street. And I was born between Eucousine, between Magnolia and Robinson.
A lot of musicians in that neighborhood when you were a kid? A lot of music?

Well, my father was a musician. What did he play? He played guitar. In fact, all my family, my uncle, on my mother's side, they was musicians out in the country, in Morripass, Louisiana. That's in Livingston Parish. And my father, he played at Tom Anderson. That was located then on North Ramport, in the 200 block of North Ramport. Same block where they, I think they have the athletic club down in there now. He played over there. What did he play with there? Well, he had his own band. And what was his name? His name was Spencer Murray. He had his own band. And he was also, he worked in the daytime, break the airport of the city.
And what about your relatives in Livingston? What were their names? Oh, Batiste. Batiste. Can you give me the instruments they played? Well, my uncle played violin. And his name? His name? His name?

His name was John Batiste. My grandfather was a guitar player. My uncle, his brother, my mother's brother is John Batiste. My grandfather's brother's name was Charlie Batiste. He was a guitar player. Both of them was guitar players. And what kind of style did they play? Well, they played the, back in that, what do you call it, real style in that time. There wasn't no jazz out there in them times. They played more reals and calling figures. That was more popular out back in those days until jazz, jazz, come up to playing jazz in New Orleans, mostly got more popular after Aura's band come in. Aura's band, under Aura's band, before Aura's band, you see, was the Silverleaf band. But Aura's band played more, but jazz had more of a swing, like we called it swing, on down, swinging of jazz music. And then, you see, the music was the music. Now, my voice playing was with the Fireman George band. A band by the name, they called him Fireman George. He was an old fireman, a volunteer fireman. And who was in that band with me was Happy Goldston. He played drum. I played the flute in the band. Lead flute player, that started.
Is that a flute like this or like this?

No, the nickel flutes. One of these nickel, you used to call it a nickel flute. Nickel flute, yeah. We played six songs as High Society and Chicken Reel. Oh, the marches on it. And what made me put on the flute was a fellow by the name of Joe Ranney, Ranney's brother. Well, they was in the home before I went out there. And he was playing, he could play flute and clarinet and he was a drummer. And he played Chicken Reel better than I did on the flute. And I said, well, I ain't playing no more flute. So I'd taken up to playing banjo, then guitar.
Well back to your parents, did your father and your relatives over there in the back each of the, did they all play fingerstyle?

Oh, yeah. Oh, no, no, no, no picking style in that time. Picking, really, Picking coming out in style and up until, well, when Nick Lucas, Nick Lucas come after making an appearance, yeah, at the shows, you know. Then he the one, first boy, picks picking down, yeah. Most fellas pick with the finger, they never use no picks to pick no get-up. No black picks. No, no, no, no, no, no kind. They didn't have no, what? Didn't have no picks. See? The fingerstyle, that was the only style that was known. Madelins, and, Madelins was in great demand, and violins, cordons, squeeze boxes, you know. There wasn't demand. And flutes, flutes was great demand back in the days. But picking with, having a pick in your hand, they didn't have no picks. No, the average fellas never picked. You're taking the bands, they pick with their hand, they never use no pick.
What about the Silver Leaf band? I ain't mentioned that.
The Silver Leaf band.
What did they play?

Well they played jazz. They played jazz? Oh yeah, Silver Leaf band, yeah. A fella by the name of Joe Nickerson, he was the late, Joe Nickerson was the guitar player in that band. And Albert Batiste was the violin player. Old man Batiste, he's passed up. But nearly all of them is there. That's none of them living.
Do you remember the other guys in the band?
No, that's all I can remember right at the present time. See? That's all I can remember of them.
Who was with Ori then? Ori?

Ori's first band. Ori's first band came here with Ori, was a fella by the name of Chiff. And his brother Stonewall. And Manuel Mineta, playing violin. And I just remember, Bob Lyons hadn't went with him yet. No.
Chiff was a Kornack player, Stonewall was a guitar player?

Yeah, his brother Stonewall was a guitar player. And Chiff was a trumpet player. And his first band came here. And then on, you know, different fellas, was a trumpet player. Well, uh... Really, the facts. You know, it's different things have come out, different papers have got their view on it. Now, uh, it's never, it's really if the truth is told, and it wouldn't do me, uh, some people tell things they hear, but I'm telling you what I know. Now, with Ori's band, when Louis became with Ori's band, I'm the man that went and got Louis. Joe Oliver quit on the corner of Padida and Franklin. He didn't have no trumpet player. Louis was nothing but a boy and was waiting for a man by the name of Spano who had a tunk at Franklin Street. And I told him, I said, if you go down there, we can get him to play. I know he can hold up. And I'm the one that went down there with him and got Louis to get working that band. See? So the truth has never been told. See, people tell us different things, you know, to go their way, but that's really the fact about it. Now, I was with him, playing up until, not playing with him, because I didn't get a chance to play with him. Get your chance to play with him again until Paul Whiteman sent me for him in 1925. I was in Chicago. See? Paul Whiteman sent me. He made one appearance. His boy singing then. That was his boy singing when he went to New York after Paul Whiteman left the Rainbow Garden. That was his boy's band. Well, after that, when I came on back down to New Orleans, I didn't see him anymore. See? Now, me and my wife, oh, we black are all raised up together. See? Come up together. Of course, she did more traveling and singing than I did. See? She worked with different shows like Florida Blossoms and different road shows, you know, and things.
What's your wife's name now?
Her name is Maddie, was, at that time, was Maddie Spencer. And they, she went in the name of Sweet. And now she's going in the name of Maddie Murray.
And who all did she sing with?

Oh, Lord, I couldn't tell you who all she had in singing. Well, I mean here. In the city here. Joe Oliver, she sing with Joe Oliver at the, where did this man here at the nightclub down on Basin Street. I can't hear, he had a nightclub on Basin Street. And he moved his night, they moved his nightclub down to Claiborne Street. P. Lala. Then she sang with Freddie Kepler up at the Rosebud, or Rosebud's Theater. That was about the first colored theater here, with entertainment. The colored entertainers working down there, was at the Rosebud. That was the whole drive between Jackson and Phillip. And that was before the lyrics started.
So she's had some good experience.

Oh, she had plenty of the Elfwaters and all of them. She had worked with all of them. She was singing and they was, what they, this is the chorus girls. Well, yeah, she's had plenty of experience about it. Really experienced about it. She followed up that until 19 and 30, she quit. Well, not, yeah, follow up the show, clean up to around 1932. That's right.
Now, you yourself, how did you get started on music?

I got started on music in school. See, I was under man, post-man started, I was going to school, I was going to school, and I was going to print and take music through an association, which was called the Louisiana Friedman, the Baptist Association, you know, of all the people. Louisiana what? Louisiana Friedman Association.
And that's where I started up my music learning, learning music.
You've been playing long when you did that? Well, I started that in 1909. And I had been playing ever since.
Well, I mean did you play the flute without lessons?
Oh, the flute without lessons, yeah. Didn't know lessons for the flute.
Well, I mean, did you play the flute without lessons?
Oh, the flute without lessons, yeah. Didn't know lessons for the flute, yeah.
When did you start on the flute?

Well, I started the flute about a year or so ahead of that. Fireman Joyce took us in and he was there. Then Dave got this choice from the home, a fellow by the name of Dave. And he'd come up and make me up a band, and that's where I went in.
What did Fireman Joyce play again after that?
He didn't play anything. He just was a volunteer fireman.
Did he sing or do anything?

No, he didn't do anything. He just was an old volunteer fireman. And I think it's around the 12th of May today would be his day to parade. And he'd have nothing but boys out there. He made up his own band. He was a voice of, well, the other way is I was into music before Happy Goldson was.
So you picked up on the music in this association. Now how did that work? Did they have a teacher there?
Yeah, Professor Dowell. He was a teacher.
And what instruments did he teach?

Well, he could teach you all instruments. All instruments. Violin. He was more specialized in violin play. And string instrument, he specializes in that. First up, we haven't got very much now as string instrument teachers. Just to a certain extent, you have, but not playing by music, or learning to read the music, well that's pretty hard. The most of the players are just from the air, playing by air, you know? It's a very few of the old players around here I have played on different occasions. You take like George Lewis, he's an old player. Howard, he's an old player that's living up to the day. But there's very few of the old ones I didn't play with. I was with Buddy P.T. Not for no, played with him, you know, for sure. Well of course, quite natural. On riffs, you know, fellas have different minds. Now you take, like no longer than yesterday. Matthews, sliding tri-bomb player. I played with him. Celestan, played with him, worked with him. Different occasions. But since they have the union now, you know, and I don't belong to the union. And he came to me yesterday. He told me, if you had your card, you go. He's going away. I think he's going to Houston. See? But, yeah.
Well now, who was in Buddy Patek's band when you were working with him?

Me and George Washington. And who else was with me and Buddy George Washington. Oh, and this Les Short-Jumma, I can't call his name. And I think Drags was playing Pace, if I'm not mistaken. And who the Clannette played, I can't recall his name now, he passed on.
About what year was it?
Oh, with Buddy? I was with Buddy around 19 and 18. 19 and 18. 19 and 18. 19 and 18.
Was this before Charny was playing with him?
Yeah. Boy over in the, Charny playing drum? Yeah, Charny played drum with me. Little Charny.
What band?
With Buddy.
With Buddy, huh?
Yeah, me, Charny, and George Washington, yeah. I told you a little short fella, I couldn't call his name at the fairs.
Was it before Zeb played clarinet or after?

Zeb was with us too. That was the clarinet player. Zeb, me, Zeb. Yeah, the same band he had. All of a sudden this boy went back and he hired him to play guitar with him. I left and went somewhere. I went away. I never just stayed around much, you know, around the all. Who did he have next?
This boy from where? From Covington.
A fella from Covington. Who's that? Buddy Manaday? Yeah, Buddy. Yeah, that's him.
Buddy. That's right.
That's Buddy. Buddy went with him after me. And I guess Edmund Hall came in on clarinet after a while too. Edmund Hall? You don't know him?
Yeah, Edmund Hall. That's right. That's right. Howl Hall would live on Washington Street's brother.
Yeah, that's right. Yeah, that's right. Yeah, he was up north. They got a picture of him with the band. Mm-hmm.
Well, he was after me.
Yeah. What was the very first band you played with on guitar?
The very first band I played on guitar? Well, banjo you say was first, huh?

Banjo, yeah. I used banjo and guitar. Yeah, I played, I had the ganjo and guitar both. Of course, the most you take, we didn't have no name, but you know, it was going to name. going to name, now you take oral, they became popular, just like silver leaf band, the golden leaf, and this boy, what is his name now, he had the on-wall band. Mani Perez. Mani Perez. Yeah. Well they had bands made up out of the jazz, they had brass bands and then they had string bands made up out of it. Now you take, the very first band I played with was, what is this, not P. Ron, oh I can't call this old clarinet player now, Blind Freddy. He's around here now. Blind Freddy had the first band I played with. Before playing with Buddy P.T.
Who was in Blind Freddy's band?

Me and Blind Freddy. Oh. I can't call all those men name at the time, right at the time they had to come to me, that's been a long time ago. Yeah. I can't call them all names, but I can't call all of them names because there was one, Brown, I remember Brown used to play slide. He played Key Slide. He's passed on. He lived upon, used to live upon Josephine, he used to play slide with us. He lived up where? Up on Josephine Street, him and Tick Chambers, you ever hear of Tick Chambers? Yeah. Yeah, well he was in the band with us, Tick Chambers. He lived up there. So that's been a good while ago. And Gabe played bass. It comes to me, you know, Gabe, Gabe, that's his name, his name was Gabriel, they call him Gabe, but he's passed on. See? And that's been a good while ago. We worked it back, I'll tell you where we worked, we worked at what they call open air, doing back, you know that Pan American, it was, now the Strait University used to be back there, but across the street from Strait University. Probably used to run an open air theater, wasn't it? Yeah. And Willie Jackson was an entertainer back there at that time, and another fella by the name of Noonie, that's way back, and Sweetie Mafius, that was an entertainer.
That was a man or a woman?
Woman, that's a woman, Sweetie Mafius. Well who was Noonie? Noonie, he was a songster.
What were they saying, him and Willie Jackson?

Well, it was mostly their own renditions, what they'd make up. They used to, they was comedians in the other way, see? And those, they understand, they never used over three or four entertainers. They didn't have no whole lot of entertainers, and flow, you know, and choruses and like that. They didn't have that master ceremonies and all sorts, but they didn't have all that. All they had was this three or four people. The biggest up shows wouldn't be over three or four people. You didn't have no whole lot of people. You might have one comedian, one songster, and that's all. And the music, and you paid. Oh, that wasn't the price, go ahead. But they made money at that, made plenty of money. Yeah, they made plenty of money at those things. That's really the fact.
What was Noonie's name?
All I know was Noonie, that's all I know.
I think they called him Noonie Johnson too.

Oh yeah, Noonie Johnson, yeah, yeah, yeah. That's the same guy? That's the same guy. He was the entertainer. That's right, Noonie Johnson. That's right. Noonie and Noonie? That was his name. That was his name. They called him Noonie. But Noonie Johnson was his name. That's him, him and Willie Jackson were the two entertainers back there. I've heard plenty about them.

Uh-huh. That's right. And I have a wonderful, well a couple of wonderful records by New Orleans Willie Jackson. Yeah. He went up north and he made some, and he made some down here too with us, Steve Lewis, just him and the piano. Yeah.
Oh Steve Lewis, yeah he used to play piano. He played piano right there. Well Steve Lewis played piano with, what is this man's name? Fredy Kaplan.
He did?
Sure. He played with P-Rone. He played with P-Rone. Who did Fredy Kaplan have winning? Oh nothing. Steve and the different guys?
Well yeah, well the most different guys.

You see, frankly, in those kind of jobs, if a fella get a job he might come to you and say, well, pass it out there. I got a job tonight, come on, play. Go ahead and play. See, it wasn't no, let's say a regular organized thing, you know, expecting your man, you just pick up anybody. See. And that's what, that kind of complicated, I was really, something that I couldn't understand when they came to saying about jazz, you know. They're writing jazz because we always had the idea if you whistle a tune and you go ahead and play behind it. But not just to say you come in and you're going to buy it and it's ruled out there. Well I don't understand the way they figured. I mean if you come in and you say, well, I want to hear you play Scotch T. I don't know, give me a little air of it. Well you get up there and you might hum anything. You hum it, well the fellas go ahead and play it. But to say you're going in a bar song or somebody setting up that writing, wasn't no writing. The fellas tell the compliment, say let's go and make play an old G and D. Don't put nothing else in there, let's play straight on chords. See. Diminishes and augments and ninths and thirteenths of chords, you didn't hear of nothing like that in those days, you know. And playing jazz. Because the average fella, he had nothing in front of him, he's not responsible. See, he playing what he think he put in there. Well you wind out, this is the St. Louis blues or some of the other blues. He's playing, he's going to put it all together. Well that's what the people wanted to hear. See. What they said is, it's different now. They said it's right to jazz, really. You couldn't be there if you want to hear a fella play it, you see.
Funny thing, those ideas they have now. What? They really changed it up now.

Well yes, they changed it up. Well, in a way, of course I go along with the public, it's just like the different styles of music you hear today, and they're saying rock and roll. And different styles. Well, the music, the publishers, it's got to sell, of course. Now you're taking, to my belief, I don't know, I might be wrong. Of course, I've had some of the music. Of course, I've had some of the music. But dear

segments.title: Recording introduction and sample songs
segments.summary: Dick Allen announces the date and place (1323 South Rampart Street, May 12, 1960); Murray sings Who's Sorry Now, C.C. Rider and I Surrender, Dear.

segments.title: Birth, New Orleans neighborhood and father Spencer Murray's band
segments.summary: Murray was born in 1896 near Eucousine Street; his father Spencer Murray played guitar and led his own band at Tom Anderson's, and his mother's family were country musicians in Livingston Parish.

segments.title: Batiste relatives and country string-band styles
segments.summary: His uncle John Batiste, grandfather and Charlie Batiste played violin and guitar, reels and calling figures, before jazz arrived; he then mentions the Fireman George boys' band.

segments.title: Playing nickel flute in Fireman George's band
segments.summary: He played lead nickel flute with Happy Goldston on drums in the volunteer fireman's band, playing marches and Chicken Reel, before switching to banjo and guitar.

segments.title: Fingerstyle guitar before picks and Nick Lucas
segments.summary: Early players used fingerstyle only; picks came after Nick Lucas, and mandolins, violins, accordions and flutes were in demand.

segments.title: The Silver Leaf band and its members
segments.summary: Murray recalls the Silver Leaf jazz band with guitarist Joe Nickerson and violinist Albert Batiste; he cannot recall others.

segments.title: Ory's first band and how Murray fetched Louis Armstrong for Oliver's band
segments.summary: Murray names Ory's first band members, then claims he got young Louis Armstrong to replace Joe Oliver, and that Paul Whiteman sent him for Louis in 1925.

segments.title: His wife Maddie's singing career in shows and theaters
segments.summary: Maddie Spencer sang with Joe Oliver, Freddie Keppard at the Rosebud theater and road shows like Florida Blossoms, until about 1932.

segments.title: Learning music through the Louisiana Freedmen Baptist Association
segments.summary: He began learning music in school through a Baptist association in 1909.

segments.title: Teaching himself flute and Fireman Joyce's boys' band
segments.summary: He played flute without lessons, joined the band organised by volunteer fireman Fireman Joyce at the home, and says he was in music before Happy Goldston.

segments.title: Professor Dowell and the decline of reading musicians
segments.summary: Professor Dowell taught all instruments, especially violin; Murray laments few string teachers and players who read, and mentions old players he worked with.

segments.title: Playing guitar in Buddy Petit's band around 1918
segments.summary: In Buddy Petit's band around 1918 were George Washington, drummer Charny, a bass player and a clarinettist.

segments.title: Clarinettist Zeb, Buddy Manaday and Edmund Hall after Murray
segments.summary: Zeb was the clarinettist; after Murray left a Covington guitarist, Buddy Manaday, followed, and Edmund Hall later came in on clarinet.

segments.title: First band on banjo and guitar: Blind Freddy's band
segments.summary: Before Buddy Petit he played banjo and guitar in Blind Freddy's band with Brown, Tick Chambers and Gabe on bass, working at an open-air theater.

segments.title: Open-air entertainers Willie Jackson, Noonie Johnson and Sweetie Mafius
segments.summary: The open-air shows had only three or four entertainers, such as songster Noonie Johnson, Willie Jackson and Sweetie Mafius, and paid well.

segments.title: Steve Lewis, Willie Jackson records and Freddie Keppard
segments.summary: Allen mentions Willie Jackson's records with Steve Lewis; Murray says Steve Lewis played piano with Freddie Keppard and Piron.

segments.title: How early jazz was played and views on rock and roll
segments.summary: Murray says jazz was improvised from a hummed tune on plain chords with no written arrangements or fancy extensions, and comments on changing styles like rock and roll.
